description: 🐸 AmphiCore Labs 🔬 is a two-person team from Dushanbe, Tajikistan, taking part in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Jonathan Sharifi leads web development, interface design, and prototyping. Benjamin Abdulaev researches NASA resources and analyzes scientific information. Together, we’re building LUNASHIFT, a lunar mission trainer where students manage limited resources and replay a mission to see how one decision changes the outcome.
summary:
LunaShift is an offline 3D educational game for children aged 7–12, developed for the “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” challenge. Players become the commander of a lunar-station shift as the base enters a period of reduced sunlight. With guidance from LUNO, a friendly robotic companion, they explore the station, complete scientific tasks, and decide how to distribute limited battery energy among plant lighting, cabin heating, communication, dust protection, research equipment, and emergency reserves.

Each decision creates visible consequences in the station and leads to different mission outcomes and achievements. The experience uses NASA research on lunar lighting, space-grown plants, communication, lunar dust, and surface exploration. Scientific phenomena are separated from simplified “LunaShift training parameters” designed for young learners.

LunaShift addresses the challenge by transforming complex mission trade-offs into an interactive story children can understand, test, and replay. It helps learners develop scientific curiosity, systems thinking, and responsible decision-making.
details:
LunaShift is an offline first-person 3D mission trainer that places children aged 7–12 in command of a lunar research station. During the mission, nearby terrain blocks sunlight from reaching the station’s solar panels. The player receives a limited battery budget and must decide how to support the greenhouse, cabin heating, communications, scientific equipment, dust protection, and reserves for the next shift.

The adventure begins with the player arriving at the lunar base and meeting LUNO, a friendly robotic mentor. LUNO explains unfamiliar concepts through short dialogue, visual examples, contextual hints, and an offline help system. The player then explores the station, learns how stored energy works, conducts a plant experiment, completes a short lunar-surface mission, collects scientific information, and sends a report to Earth. Finally, the player creates an energy plan for the shadow period.

The player’s decisions change the station visually. Plant lights activate, equipment responds, the antenna transmits data, battery reserves decrease, and the mission reaches one of several possible outcomes. Instead of giving one score or punishing mistakes, LunaShift explains the effects on three areas: crew and plant care, scientific work, and readiness for the next shift. Players can replay the mission, test another plan, unlock achievements, and compare the consequences.

NASA resources provide the scientific foundation for the experience. These include lunar-lighting visualizations, space-plant research, Delay-Tolerant Networking, lunar dust-mitigation technology, and lunar-surface research. NASA evidence explains the real phenomena, while simplified energy values are clearly identified as “LunaShift training parameters.” This prevents the educational model from being presented as an exact operational simulation.

We developed the prototype with TypeScript, React, Vite, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, i18next, and Electron. The result is a downloadable Windows application that works without an internet connection. It includes English and Russian localization, adjustable text size, high-contrast options, reduced-motion settings, graphics-quality modes, keyboard controls, and contextual assistance.

LunaShift is creative because it teaches science through responsibility and visible consequences. Children do not simply read facts or answer a quiz. They explore a story, make meaningful decisions, and observe how connected systems affect one another. Our team considered scientific accuracy, child-friendly language, accessibility, performance on ordinary computers, replayability, data-source transparency, and the need to make complex engineering trade-offs understandable without removing their importance.

Our intended impact is to help young learners develop scientific curiosity, systems thinking, and confidence in decision-making while experiencing the excitement and responsibility of managing a mission beyond Earth.
